name: Joh. Jos. Prüm Wehlener Sonnenuhr Riesling Spätlese 2015
text:
## Joh. Jos. Prüm Wehlener Sonnenuhr Riesling Spätlese 2015

**The story.** Weingut Joh. Jos. Prüm is based in [Wehlen](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Weingut+Joh.+Jos.+Pr%C3%BCm,+Bernkastel-Wehlen,+Germany&t=k), now part of [Bernkastel-Kues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernkastel-Kues) on the Middle [Mosel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosel_%28wine_region%29). The Prüm family has been in Wehlen for over 400 years; this estate was founded in 1911 by Johann Josef Prüm when the family's holdings were split. His son Sebastian, who joined in 1920, built its reputation: Robert Parker credits him with developing "the distinct style of the Prüm wines during the 1930s and 1940s". Sebastian's son Dr Manfred Prüm took over in 1969 and was German Winemaker of the Year in 1996; his daughter Dr Katharina Prüm has worked with him since 2003 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weingut_Joh._Jos._Pr%C3%BCm)).

The estate grows only [Riesling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesling), on 14 hectares in the Wehlener Sonnenuhr, Graacher Himmelreich, Bernkasteler Lay, Bernkasteler Badstube and Zeltinger Sonnenuhr vineyards, and 70% of its vines are ungrafted. Stuart Pigott writes that "since the early 1920s its wines have been among Germany's best Rieslings", and Stephen Brook calls them "the epitome of filigree elegance: light in body but intense in flavour, exquisitely balanced and precisely tuned, and capable of the most extra-ordinary longevity" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weingut_Joh._Jos._Pr%C3%BCm)).

**The vineyard: Wehlener Sonnenuhr.** "Sonnenuhr" means [sundial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundial). The story goes that in the 1840s Jodocus Prüm painted a sundial on a rocky outcrop in the middle of this steep slope, so the vineyard workers could tell the time; the vineyard took its name, and today it is split among some 200 separate owners, several of them Prüm descendants ([Vinography](https://www.vinography.com/2009/09/2007_sa_prum_wehlener_sonnenuh)). It is J.J. Prüm's most important site, in quantity and quality ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weingut_Joh._Jos._Pr%C3%BCm)), and Stephan Reinhardt calls this Spätlese "the legendary number one" among the estate's classics.

**What Spätlese means.** [Spätlese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_wine_classification) means "late harvest": in Germany's ripeness-based system, the wine's category depends on how ripe the grapes were. J.J. Prüm Spätlese is a fruity, sweet style balanced by the Mosel's racy acidity, and famous for ageing for decades.

**The vintage.** [Jancis Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jancis_Robinson)'s [Germany vintage chart](https://www.jancisrobinson.com/learn/vintages/germany) says 2015 was "especially promising" in the Mosel, though yields were 8% below 2014.

**What the critics say for 2015.** As listed by [Farr Vintners](https://www.farrvintners.com/wine.php?wine=44763) and [Justerini & Brooks](https://www.justerinis.com/fine-wines/germany/mosel-saar-ruwer/jj-prum/wehlener-sonnenuhr-riesling-spatlese/2015):
- **[James Suckling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Suckling): 95** (May 2017). "Probably the finest 2015 spätlese from J.J. Prum", though the nose was still closed; "sensational clarity and vibrancy on the palate", with a super-long, refined mineral finish and "a long future ahead of it".
- **[Vinous](https://vinous.com): 94** (Neal Martin). It "hardly seems to have aged since bottling": apricot blossom and mint, linear and tensile, "built around its razor-sharp acidity", with wild peach on a finish "that just fizzes with energy". "This will blossom over 40 or 50 years with no problem."
- **[Wine Advocate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wine_Advocate): 93** (Stephan Reinhardt, April 2017). A clear, fine, floral bouquet of white fruits, flowers and weathered slate; sweet, lush and juicy, with piquant acidity and a tight but elegant structure. "A gorgeous Spätlese" with more sweetness and charm than the estate's Zeltinger Sonnenuhr.
- **Mosel Fine Wines: 93** (Jean Fisch and David Rayer, October 2016). Yellow fruits, white flowers, melon and grapefruit; smooth, with playful acidity and fresh herbs. Drink 2025 to 2045.
- **[CellarTracker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CellarTracker) community: 92.6** (from your CellarTracker list).

**How it's drinking now.** In October 2026 the wine is eleven years old. Your CellarTracker list gives a window of 2023 to 2041; Mosel Fine Wines suggests 2025 to 2045, and Vinous 40 or 50 years. Vinous found it had hardly aged at all by its review. So it is just entering its window, and will reward patience for decades. Serve at 8 to 10°C, and give a younger bottle half an hour in the glass.

**Food.** Classic with spicy Asian food (Thai, Vietnamese, Sichuan), roast pork with apples, smoked trout, or a mild blue cheese; and perfect on its own.

**Value and where to buy.** J.J. Prüm is easy to find on this site: BSW Liquor has the 2023 Wehlener Sonnenuhr Spätlese at $105, the Graacher Himmelreich Spätlese at $94.99 and Kabinett at $87.99, and the Wehlener Sonnenuhr Kabinett 2020 at $112; BC Liquor has the 2018 Graacher Himmelreich Spätlese at $88.99 and Auslese at $92.99; ZYN has the 2020 Bernkasteler Lay Auslese at $96.

**From the history books**
- **A family of winemakers.** When Jodocus Prüm's health failed in the late 1800s, he divided his land among his seven children; today at least seven wineries carry the Prüm name, including S.A. Prüm ([Vinography](https://www.vinography.com/2009/09/2007_sa_prum_wehlener_sonnenuh)).
- **The great Mosel.** The Mosel is Germany's third-largest region by production, but some consider it the leading one for prestige; until 2007 it was called Mosel-Saar-Ruwer ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosel_%28wine_region%29)).
- **A philosopher's town.** Neighbouring Bernkastel-Kues was the birthplace of the medieval churchman and philosopher [Nicholas of Cusa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_of_Cusa) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernkastel-Kues)).

**Curious details**
- **The world's steepest vineyard.** The Mosel is famous for vertiginous slopes: the Calmont, at 65°, is the steepest recorded vineyard in the world ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosel_%28wine_region%29)).
- **Ungrafted vines.** Seventy percent of J.J. Prüm's vines are ungrafted, on their own roots, rather than grafted onto rootstocks that resist [phylloxera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phylloxera) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weingut_Joh._Jos._Pr%C3%BCm)).
